sources.note: Exact live id, display label, culture kind, approximate 1500 BCE to 1700 lifetime and historical-basemaps provenance.

sources.title: Human History Map research coverage ledger
sources.note: Thirty exact observed intervals, thirty border files, missing summary and card, and initially unreviewed identity, chronology and borders.

sources.title: Human History Map 1500 BCE borders
sources.note: Exact twenty-five-part geometry, bounds, checksum and tested island and mainland point owners for 1500 to 1000 BCE.

sources.title: Human History Map 800 CE borders
sources.note: Documents the sharp reduction to four components and seams with Ciboney and Arawaks atlas labels.

sources.title: Human History Map 1000 CE borders
sources.note: Documents the three-part geometry and seams with Taíno and Arawaks atlas labels.

sources.title: Human History Map 1400 CE borders
sources.note: Contains two separate exact-id Polygon features, including Paria and an Amazon-mouth component, beside Taíno and Kalinago labels.

sources.title: Human History Map 1492 CE borders
sources.note: Retains only the small mainland component while named Indigenous island layers occupy tested island points.

sources.title: Human History Map 1500 CE borders
sources.note: Restores three target components including Barbados and Paria in an editorial reversal after the 1492 snapshot.

sources.title: Human History Map 1530 CE borders
sources.note: Reduces the target to two mainland components while colonial and named Indigenous labels own tested island and Paria points.

sources.title: Human History Map 1650 CE borders
sources.note: Retains one small Amazon-mouth Polygon through the final exact interval with increased map precision.

sources.title: Human History Map 1700 CE borders
sources.note: Confirms exact-id disappearance at the indexed endpoint while peoples, communities and colonial struggles continue.

sources.title: Introduction to The Archaeology of the Caribbean
sources.note: Regional archaeological synthesis emphasizes early seafaring, long occupation, mainland contacts and changing island economies.

sources.title: Archaeology of the Caribbean Region
sources.note: Regional synthesis treats the Caribbean Sea as a connected maritime basin rather than isolated islands.

sources.title: Verification of an Archaic Age occupation on Barbados
sources.note: Radiocarbon study verifies an early occupation on Barbados and demonstrates the value of direct dating.

sources.title: Earliest phase of settlement in the eastern Caribbean
sources.note: Montserrat excavations and dates revise early eastern-Caribbean settlement models and connect sites to chert resources.

sources.title: Diversity of Lifeways in Early Antillean Societies
sources.note: Multi-isotope study of 146 people from eight Cuban sites reveals diverse diet and mobility rather than one lifeway.

sources.title: First Lithic Age Caribbean genomes
sources.note: A clearly labeled 2026 preprint reports four early genomes, local structure and long continuity while stressing limited sampling.

sources.title: A genetic history of the pre-contact Caribbean
sources.note: Genome-wide study of 174 ancient people finds multiple ancestries, mobility, relatives across islands and living continuity.

sources.title: Origins and genetic legacies of the Caribbean Taíno
sources.note: Lucayan genome study finds continuity with present-day Caribbean people while rejecting simplistic extinction narratives.

sources.title: Where are the Caribs? Ancient DNA from the Lesser Antilles
sources.note: Ancient-DNA study demonstrates how colonial ethnic labels and archaeological categories can mislead biological interpretation.

sources.title: Edible flora in pre-Columbian Caribbean coprolites
sources.note: Plant DNA and starch evidence identifies diverse foods while explaining preservation, processing and identification limits.

sources.title: Molecular evidence for new foodways in the early colonial Caribbean
sources.note: Organic-residue study at Isla de Mona reveals Indigenous vessel use and coerced colonial intensification of cassava production.

sources.title: Dental-calculus microbiome of pre-Columbian Puerto Rico
sources.note: Dental calculus preserves microbial and dietary evidence while requiring careful contamination controls and local interpretation.

sources.title: Isotopic reconstruction of weaning at Canímar Abajo
sources.note: Bayesian isotope models reconstruct one Cuban community’s breastfeeding and complementary-food sequence without universalizing it.

sources.title: Paleodietary reconstruction of endemic rodents in the Dominican Republic
sources.note: Isotopes distinguish wild hutia feeding from human-shaped niches and illuminate human-animal relations around settlements.

sources.title: Pre-Columbian zoonotic enteric parasites in Puerto Rico
sources.note: Microscopy, DNA and animal bones reveal parasites and food exposure in specific Vieques archaeological contexts.

sources.title: Paleomicrobiology of ancient Indigenous Caribbean coprolites
sources.note: Metagenomics of Vieques coprolites investigates gut microbes, diet and parasite loads while noting tropical preservation problems.

sources.title: Archaeology, environmental justice and climate change on Caribbean islands
sources.note: Long-term comparison links storms, freshwater limits, settlement choices and rapidly repairable Indigenous architecture.

sources.title: Resilience in pre-Columbian Caribbean house-building
sources.note: House-post patterns show locally adapted architecture and caution against importing continental or chronicler descriptions.

sources.title: Archaeology, historical ecology and anthropogenic island ecosystems
sources.note: Reviews varied Caribbean human impacts, transported species, fishing and long-term resource management.

sources.title: Island Rhythms: interaction networks in the Lesser Antilles
sources.note: Artifact sourcing reconstructs overlapping exchange rhythms for tools, identity markers and ceremonial valuables.

sources.title: Reimagining Creolization in the Windward Islands
sources.note: Material culture documents mobility, alliances and Indigenous adaptation through the colonial period.

sources.title: Roots of the Columbian Exchange
sources.note: Network analysis shows early encounter transactions entering older Indigenous systems of value before relations became coercive.

sources.title: Indigenous Caribbean perspectives and legacies
sources.note: Community-engaged archaeology documents homes, exchange, colonial disruption, survival and descendant perspectives.

sources.title: Jamaican Taíno settlement configuration
sources.note: House plans and terraces test local family residence and labor organization rather than assuming a universal household.

sources.title: Biographies of bodily ornaments in the Dominican Republic
sources.note: Contextual study follows ornaments through houses, refuse, burials and changing colonial lives.

sources.title: Taíno ritual seat from Hispaniola
sources.note: British Museum object record documents material, imagery, provenance and cautious dating of a carved wooden duho.

sources.title: Ball-court petroglyph boulders at Jacaná
sources.note: Detailed recording places Puerto Rican rock imagery in archaeological and ethnohistorical context without treating it as deciphered text.

sources.title: Taíno: Native Heritage and Identity in the Caribbean gallery guide
sources.note: Smithsonian educational guide centers living Taíno identity, material culture, food, healing and the absence of pre-contact writing.

sources.title: Caribbean Indigenous Legacies Project
sources.note: Smithsonian project presents Taíno culture as a living, community-defined legacy rather than an extinct past.

sources.title: The Arawakan Matrix
sources.note: Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute volume compares Arawakan-speaking societies while warning against flattening historical diversity.

sources.title: Wars of invasion in the Caribbean and Mesoamerica, 1492 to 1547
sources.note: Historical synthesis analyzes conquest warfare, Indigenous resistance and the violent creation of colonial rule.

sources.title: Slave raiders versus friars in Tierra Firme, 1513 to 1522
sources.note: Study of Tierra Firme exposes raiding, mission politics and colonial manufacture of hostile Carib categories.

sources.title: Why Indigenous slavery continued after the New Laws of 1542
sources.note: Explains legal loopholes, war captives and continuing enslavement despite nominal prohibition.

sources.title: Contested conquests: African maroons and Hispaniola
sources.note: Shows colonial power remained incomplete amid African maroon resistance and shifting Indigenous alliances.

sources.title: Reconsidering Taíno social dynamics after Spanish conquest
sources.note: Household archaeology at En Bas Saline examines gender, class and persistence under Spanish domination.

sources.title: Where strangers met at LaSoye Point, Dominica
sources.note: Storm-exposed deposits combine Cayo pottery and European goods at an early colonial trading place.

sources.title: The Indigenous People: Kalinagos
sources.note: Dominica cultural authority presents Kalinago history, names, resistance and living community.

sources.title: The Kalinago Territory today
sources.note: Dominica cultural authority documents present governance, crafts, farming, boat building and cultural continuity.

sources.title: Caribbean Archaeology and the World Heritage Convention
sources.note: UNESCO regional volume emphasizes diverse archaeological cultures, daily life and intangible Indigenous heritage.

sources.title: Medicinal Plants of the Guianas
sources.note: Smithsonian ethnobotanical compilation offers later comparative knowledge, not direct proof of ancient treatment.

sources.title: Ethnoarchaeology of settlement sanitation in French Guiana
sources.note: Later ethnoarchaeological comparison distinguishes drains, latrines, dumps and other settlement features.

proposedOverrides.summary: A carefully bounded guide to the many island and northern South American communities hidden under the atlas’s shifting “Caribbean hunter-gatherers” umbrella, covering food, canoes, homes, families, health, toilets, colonial violence and living continuity from 1500 BCE to 1700.
